source: US headlines use the word sue significantly more than those from India, South Africa, or the UK, where suing may be a less common practice.
claim: The word 'sue' appears in 170 headlines from the USA, more than in the UK (109), India (75) or South Africa (21).

source: Muslim appears more frequently in Indian headlines, compared to the UK, the US, and South Africa, as local news in India often reports the religion of the story’s subject.
claim: The word 'Muslim' appears in 1,293 headlines from India, more than in the UK (489), the USA (340) or South Africa (22).

source: the use of many gendered words (e.g.“sexy,” “fat,” “housewife” or “gossip”) has faded out over time
claim: The share of headlines containing 'sexy' falls from 1.16% in 2005 to 0.05% in 2021, 'fat' from a peak of 0.57% in 2008 to 0.05%, 'housewife' from 0.58% in 2005 to 0.01%, and 'gossip' from a peak of 1.69% in 2009 to 0.20%.

source: the use of empowering words has increased over time (e.g. “founder,” “activist,” “leader” or “appoint”)
claim: The share of headlines containing 'founder' rises from 0.02% in 2010 to 0.12% in 2021, 'activist' from 0.02% to 0.28%, 'leader' from 0.04% to 0.26%, and 'appoint' from 0.00% to 0.05%.

source: Other words (e.g. “death,” “hurt,” and “drama”) have instead stood the test of time, as their use has remained consistent since 2005.
claim: The share of headlines containing 'death' ranges from 1.68% in 2011 to 3.51% in 2007 and is 2.16% in 2021, while 'hurt' peaks at 0.18% in 2011 and 'drama' at 0.18% in 2009.

source: That was part of a wave of increased trans visibility that helps to explain why “transgender” shot up in 2015.
claim: The share of headlines containing 'transgender' rises from 0.27% in 2014 to 0.74% in 2015.

source: That adds context to the sharp rise of “harassment” in 2017
claim: The share of headlines containing 'harassment' rises from 0.33% in 2016 to 0.69% in 2017.
